title: Investigation into use of Tasers is right for both police and public
article: There are serious questions about police use of Tasers, and there are equally serious questions about why the Vancouver Police Department took a full month to inform the public that Robert Bagnell had died after being shocked with a Taser.
Now, thanks to B.C. police complaints commissioner Dirk Ryneveld, it looks like we'll find the answers to those questions.
On Thursday, Mr. Ryneveld ordered an investigation into Mr. Bagnell's death and the use of Tasers, in part because the police failed to notify Mr. Bagnell's family that a Taser was used.

Mr. Ryneveld called for an external investigation -- to be led by Victoria Police Chief Paul Battershill -- because he said Vancouver Police Chief Jamie Graham made comments about the case that compromised his impartiality.
We're pleased with Mr. Ryneveld's decision for two reasons.

First, the police have never offered a cogent reason for the delay in stating that Mr. Bagnell died after being shocked with a Taser gun. Chief Graham said police were waiting for toxicology reports to see what caused Mr. Bagnell's death, yet only a pathology report determines the cause of death, and police didn't wait for that report.

Second, although many healthy people have suffered no ill effects after having been shocked with Tasers, it's not clear what effect they have on people who are in poor health or are high on drugs -- precisely the people often subjected to a Taser strike.

Mr. Ryneveld made the right decision in calling for the investigation, because it's in the best interest of both the police and public to review police procedures and to gain more information about the possible harmful effects of Tasers.
